name: Padamchen
tagline: A forest halt on the Silk Route, one step below Zuluk
meta_description: Padamchen on the Old Silk Route: forest homestays at about 2,000 m between Rongli and Zuluk, birds, rhododendrons, permits, prices and when to go.
summary: Padamchen is a small forest village at roughly 2,000 m on the Silk Route road between Rongli and Zuluk in East Sikkim. It is a quiet first night on the climb: a few family homestays at about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals, dense forest, birds at dawn and an easier height for the body before Zuluk and Gnathang.

local_story.title: The forest stretch of the Lhasa road
paras: Before Gangtok's road over Nathu La took over, the busiest track between India and Tibet ran from Kalimpong to Pedong, Rhenock and Rongli, then climbed through the forest towards Zuluk and over Jelep La. Padamchen sits on that climb, in the wooded middle section where the road leaves the warm river valley around Rongli and starts gaining height in earnest. Mule trains carrying Tibetan wool down to Kalimpong, and cloth, salt and tools up to the Chumbi valley, passed through these slopes for decades before the trade stopped after 1959 and the border closed in 1962.

For the next half century this was army country, and the road was kept open mainly for the forces posted towards the passes. The forest around Padamchen became part of the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary when it was notified in 2002, which is why the slopes here are still thick with oak, rhododendron and bamboo rather than terraces. When travellers began coming back for the Silk Route in the 2010s, mostly families from Bengal driving up for the Zuluk loops, a few households in Padamchen opened rooms. Today it is the softer night of the circuit: lower, a little warmer and quieter than Zuluk.

did_you_know: Padamchen lies inside the landscape of the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, notified in 2002, which runs from about 1,760 m up to 4,390 m along the Sikkim–Bhutan–Tibet border country.
At roughly 2,000 m, Padamchen is about 900 m lower than Zuluk, which makes it a gentler first night for anyone driving up from the plains in a single day.
The road through Padamchen follows the line of the Raj-era Kalimpong–Lhasa trade route, which crossed into Tibet at Jelep La, about 4,390 m.
intro: Padamchen is easy to miss. The Silk Route road from Rongli climbs through thick forest, passes a few houses, an army establishment and a cluster of homestays, and then carries on to Zuluk. Most cars stop only for tea. We think it deserves a night, for two plain reasons: it sits at about 2,000 m, a sensible height to sleep at before the 3,000–4,000 m stretch above, and the forest around it is the best-preserved part of the whole circuit. Mornings here are for birds, mist and the sound of streams, not for sights.

The practical side is the same as for the rest of the Silk Route. Indian travellers need the Silk Route permit issued at Rongli, and almost everyone comes in a reserved car, because shared transport above Rongli is scarce. Homestays cost about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with dinner and breakfast. Rooms are simple and nights are cool even in summer. Landslides can block the road between June and September and snow can reach it in a hard winter. Check current status before you travel.
facts: Forest homestays, birds, a gentle first night on the Silk Route
costs: Reserved SUV for the Silk Route
Small fee; agents may add a handling charge
Noodles or thukpa at a roadside shop

highlights.title: A gentler height to sleep at
highlights.text: At roughly 2,000 m, Padamchen lets the body adjust before Zuluk at about 2,900 m and the passes at about 4,000 m. Families with children and older travellers who drive up from Siliguri or Gangtok in one day often sleep better here than higher up.

highlights.title: The forest of Pangolakha
highlights.text: The slopes around Padamchen fall within the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, notified in 2002. Oak, rhododendron, magnolia and bamboo crowd the road, streams cross it at every bend, and the forest stays green when the higher slopes have turned brown in winter.

highlights.title: Dawn birds on the road
highlights.text: Early mornings bring mixed flocks of tits, laughingthrushes and minivets along the forest edge, and pheasants are possible on quiet stretches. Walk the road slowly between 6 and 8 am with binoculars, staying on the hill side and watching for army trucks.

highlights.title: Rhododendrons in spring
highlights.text: From March to May the forest between Padamchen and Zuluk flowers in red, pink and white, lower down first and higher up later. It is the season we like best for this stretch, with long days and the road usually open.

highlights.title: A short hop to Zuluk
highlights.text: Zuluk and its zigzag road are about 12–15 km further up, under an hour by car. From a Padamchen base you can drive up for Thambi View Point and come back, or move on to Zuluk for the dawn trip to Lungthung.

how_to_reach.text: Take a shared jeep from Gangtok to Rongli, about 69 km and 2.5–3 h, for ₹200–300 a seat. After the permit is done, a car arranged by your homestay covers the last 18–20 km to Padamchen, about an hour. This is the cheapest way for solo travellers and couples.

Most travellers hire an SUV for the whole Silk Route from Gangtok, Siliguri or NJP at about ₹5,000–7,000 a day. The driver usually arranges the Rongli permit in advance with your ID copies and photos. From Siliguri the drive is about 120–130 km and 5 h via Rangpo and Rongli.

When NH10 along the Teesta is closed, as it has often been since the October 2023 flood, cars come up from Siliguri through Kalimpong, Pedong and Rhenock to Rongli, the old trade route. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Padamchen has no hotels, only a handful of family homestays along the road. Rooms are plain, usually with attached or shared bathrooms, thick quilts and hot water by bucket or geyser depending on the house. Rates of about ₹1,200–1,800 per person include dinner and breakfast: rice, dal, a vegetable, eggs or chicken, and noodles or parathas in the morning. There are few houses, so book ahead in October, November and the April–May season, usually through a Silk Route driver or a Gangtok agent. If Padamchen is full, the homestays of Zuluk higher up are the obvious alternative.
tips: Carry four photocopies of your photo ID and four passport photos per person for the Rongli permit and the checkpoints beyond.
Draw enough cash in Gangtok or Rangpo, because there is no ATM you can rely on beyond Rongli.
Ask your homestay to confirm the booking by phone the day before, since signal in Padamchen can disappear for hours.
Pack a fleece and a warm hat even in May, because forest nights at 2,000 m are cool and damp.
Use Padamchen as the first night and Zuluk as the second, rather than the other way round, so you climb gradually.

experiences.title: A first night in the forest at 2,000 m
experiences.summary: Break the Silk Route climb with a night in a Padamchen family homestay, about 900 m below Zuluk. You get a home-cooked dinner, a quiet forest night and an easier start to the higher road the next morning.
body: The usual Silk Route plan is to drive from Gangtok or Siliguri straight to Zuluk in one day. It works, but it means going from the plains to about 2,900 m in a few hours, and some people pay for it with a headache and a bad night. Stopping at Padamchen, roughly 2,000 m, softens that jump. You arrive in the afternoon, walk a little along the road, and sit down to dinner with the family in a kitchen that is usually the warmest room in the house.

The homestays here are small and simple. Expect a wooden or concrete house, two to four guest rooms, heavy quilts and hot water by bucket on cold days. Meals are the household's own food: rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable such as squash or mustard greens, eggs or chicken, and perhaps local pickles. Breakfast is noodles, parathas or puri. Rates of about ₹1,200–1,800 per person include both meals. Tell your hosts in advance if you are vegetarian.

Use the evening to ask about the road ahead. Families here know when the upper road was last closed, which bends are being repaired and whether snow has fallen at Gnathang. Go to bed early; drivers often want to leave by 7 am to reach Zuluk and Thambi View Point in clear morning light. If anyone feels unwell, Padamchen is also a good place to stay put an extra night rather than going higher.

faqs.q: Is Padamchen better than Zuluk for the first night?
faqs.a: For most people driving up in a single day, yes. Padamchen is about 900 m lower than Zuluk, so the body copes more easily, and it is only about an hour's drive below. You can still reach Thambi View Point early the next morning and sleep in Zuluk on the second night if you wish.

faqs.q: How much does a Padamchen homestay cost?
faqs.a: Expect about ₹1,200–1,800 per person a night, including dinner and breakfast. Rates rise a little in October, November and the spring holidays, and some homestays charge extra for a heater or extra quilts. Agents and drivers who book for you may add their margin, so ask what is included before you pay.

faqs.q: Do Padamchen homestays have hot water and electricity?
faqs.a: Most have electricity, though cuts are common, and hot water by geyser or by bucket. Do not expect heating beyond quilts and perhaps an electric heater. Carry a torch and a power bank, and ask about hot water timings on arrival, because some houses heat it only in the morning and evening.

experiences.title: Dawn birds on the Pangolakha forest road
experiences.summary: A slow early walk along the forest road around Padamchen, inside the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary landscape. Mixed flocks of small forest birds are common at first light; pheasants are a lucky bonus. Bring binoculars and keep to the road.
body: Padamchen sits in the lower, wetter part of the Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, notified in 2002. Here the forest is broadleaf and dense: oak, rhododendron, magnolia, maples and bamboo, dripping with moss and ferns. That habitat suits the mixed bird flocks of the eastern Himalaya, which move through the canopy in loose groups soon after sunrise. You hear them before you see them, so stop often, stand still and let them come past.

There are no forest trails open for casual visitors here, and there is no need for one. Walk a kilometre or two of the road in either direction from the village between 6 and 8 am, when traffic is light. Look along the forest edge and in gaps where streams cross the road. Laughingthrushes, tits, minivets, sunbirds and flycatchers are the common company. Kalij pheasant sometimes cross quiet stretches, and blood pheasant live higher up towards Zuluk.

Bring binoculars, a light rain jacket and a warm layer, because early mornings are damp. Walk on the hill side of the road and step well off it when army trucks or Silk Route cars come round a bend. Leeches can appear on wet verges in late spring. Do not use playback calls, do not leave the road to follow birds into the forest, and keep voices low. Back at the homestay, breakfast will be waiting.

faqs.q: What birds can you see at Padamchen?
faqs.a: The common sightings are mixed flocks of laughingthrushes, tits, minivets, sunbirds and flycatchers in the broadleaf forest. Kalij pheasant are possible on quiet stretches, and blood pheasant and Himalayan monal live higher up towards Zuluk and Thambi. March to May is the best season, with October and November close behind.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for birding at Padamchen?
faqs.a: Not for a walk along the road, which is covered by the Silk Route permit Indian travellers get at Rongli. A local guide is useful but not always available; ask your homestay. Entering the sanctuary forest away from the road may need forest department permission, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there leeches at Padamchen?
faqs.a: Leeches can be active on wet verges and forest paths from late spring through the monsoon, roughly May to September. Wear closed shoes and long socks, tuck trousers in, and check your legs after a walk. A little salt removes them. In October and November leeches are much less of a problem.

experiences.title: Walking the rhododendron stretch in spring
experiences.summary: In spring the forest above Padamchen flowers in red, pink and white. Walk a few kilometres of the Silk Route road uphill through the blooms and have your car pick you up further on. Easy walking, good light before cloud, and very few people.
body: From March to May the road between Padamchen and Zuluk passes through some of the best rhododendron forest on the Silk Route. The flowering starts lower down in March with the tree rhododendrons and moves uphill through April and May, so at any point in the season there is usually a band of colour somewhere on the climb. The red blooms of the tree rhododendron are the most common; pinks and creams appear higher up.

The simplest plan is to start walking uphill from the village after breakfast and ask your driver to follow an hour later and collect you wherever you have reached. The road is paved, the gradient is steady rather than steep, and 4–6 km takes most people two to three hours with stops. Morning is better than afternoon, because cloud often rises from the valley by midday and the light goes flat.

Carry water, a rain shell and a snack. Walk on the hill side, in single file, and step aside for vehicles. Do not pick flowers or break branches; the forest is within a wildlife sanctuary and local families take its protection seriously. Some years the flowering is thin or late after a cold winter, so treat any guarantee from an agent with care, and check current status of the road before you travel.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom around Padamchen?
faqs.a: Usually from late March to May, starting lower down and moving uphill as spring advances. Mid-April is often the best time around Padamchen and Zuluk, with flowers higher up into May. The timing shifts with the weather each year, so ask your homestay a week or two before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk on the Silk Route road?
faqs.a: Yes, for short stretches by day, if you are careful. Walk in single file on the hill side, step well off the road for army trucks and cars, and avoid walking in fog or after dark. Do not walk close to the outer edge, which can be unstable after rain.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Padamchen to Zuluk?
faqs.a: Zuluk is roughly 12–15 km up the road from Padamchen, with a big climb of about 900 m. Few people walk all of it. We suggest walking 4–6 km through the best forest and letting your car pick you up for the rest of the climb.

experiences.title: A morning hop up to Zuluk and Thambi
experiences.cost: Included in your Silk Route car
experiences.summary: From a Padamchen base, drive up early past Zuluk to Thambi View Point for the famous loops of the Silk Route road, then come back down or carry on. It turns Padamchen into a practical base for the whole lower circuit.
body: Padamchen works well as a base because the main sight of the lower Silk Route is close. Zuluk is less than an hour up the road, and Thambi View Point, at about 3,400 m, is a short drive beyond it. From Thambi you look down on the road folding back on itself in tier after tier of hairpins, the view that made this route famous. Leave Padamchen by about 7 am to arrive before cloud comes up from the valleys.

Many travellers make this the first leg of the second day: Padamchen to Thambi for the loops, on to Lungthung if time and weather allow, then back to Zuluk or Gnathang for the night. Others with only one night use it as a there-and-back trip before returning to Rongli and Gangtok. Either way, take it slowly, because you are gaining about 1,400 m in a morning.

Dress for wind and cold at Thambi in every month. Carry water and snacks, as stalls open only in the main seasons. The stop is covered by your Silk Route permit and your car hire; there is no entry fee. From December to March snow can close the upper road, and in the monsoon landslides may. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Thambi View Point from Padamchen?
faqs.a: Thambi View Point is roughly 20–25 km above Padamchen, past Zuluk, usually about 1–1.5 hours by car depending on the road. It sits at about 3,400 m, so you climb around 1,400 m. Leave early, by about 7 am, to see the loops before cloud rises.

faqs.q: Can we see the Zuluk loops on a day trip from Padamchen?
faqs.a: Yes. Many travellers sleep at Padamchen, drive up to Thambi View Point early in the morning and come back the same day, or continue to Zuluk for a second night. The trip is covered by the Silk Route permit and your car hire, with no separate entry fee.

faqs.q: Is the road above Padamchen open in winter?
faqs.a: Often, but not always. Snow from December to March can close the road above Zuluk for days, and chains may be needed. Landslides are the main risk from June to September. Ask your homestay the evening before and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where is Padamchen?
faqs.a: Padamchen is a small forest village on the Silk Route road in East Sikkim, between Rongli and Zuluk. It sits at roughly 2,000 m, about 18–20 km above Rongli and around 12–15 km below Zuluk. Most travellers pass through it on the way to the Zuluk loops; a few stay a night in its family homestays.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Padamchen?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian travellers need the Silk Route permit issued at Rongli, which covers Padamchen, Zuluk and the road beyond. Drivers and homestays usually arrange it with copies of photo ID and passport photos. Foreign nationals face separate and often stricter rules. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I reach Padamchen from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Padamchen is about 85–90 km from Gangtok via Rongli, roughly 3.5–4 hours. Take a shared jeep to Rongli for ₹200–300 a seat and a homestay car beyond, or hire an SUV for the whole Silk Route at about ₹5,000–7,000 a day.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Padamchen?
faqs.a: October and November bring clear skies and dry roads, and March to May brings rhododendrons and birdsong. December to February is cold, with occasional snow on the road above. June to September is the monsoon, with leeches, mist and landslide risk, and we suggest avoiding it.

faqs.q: Should we stay at Padamchen or Zuluk?
faqs.a: If you can, both: Padamchen on the first night and Zuluk on the second. Padamchen is lower, at roughly 2,000 m, so it is easier on the body and warmer. Zuluk is closer to Thambi and Lungthung for the early-morning trips. With only one night, Zuluk is the usual choice.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM or mobile network at Padamchen?
faqs.a: There is no ATM at Padamchen, and we would not rely on one beyond Rongli. Mobile signal is weak and patchy, with long gaps on the road. Carry cash for homestays, food, permits and tips, and tell family your plans before you leave Rongli.

faqs.q: Is Padamchen good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes, it is one of the better places on the Silk Route for families, because the height of roughly 2,000 m is easier than Zuluk or Gnathang. The homestays are simple, so pack warm clothes, snacks and any medicines. Keep children away from the road edge on walks.

faqs.q: Does it snow at Padamchen?
faqs.a: Padamchen gets snow only in some winters, usually a light fall between late December and February. The road above, towards Zuluk, Thambi and Gnathang, gets more snow and for longer. Snow can close the upper road, so keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is there to do in Padamchen?
faqs.a: Padamchen is for slowing down. Walk the forest road at dawn for birds, see rhododendrons in spring, eat home-cooked meals with your hosts, and use it as a base for a morning trip to Zuluk and Thambi View Point. There are no shops beyond small tea stalls.
